cards.title: Question 1
cards.stim: Researchers engineer a variant of a digestive enzyme by substituting two surface residues. Initial reaction rates were measured for the wild-type (WT) and variant enzymes at saturating substrate and pH 7.4.
cards.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by Figure 1?
opts: A. The variant lowers activation energy more than WT does at every temperature tested.
B. The variant remains folded and catalytically competent at higher temperatures than WT does.
C. The variant binds substrate with higher affinity, which explains its higher rate at 50 °C and 60 °C.
D. WT is already denatured at 40 °C, whereas the variant is not.

key.rationale: WT peaks at 40 °C and falls at 50–60 °C, while the variant peaks near 50 °C: the denaturation-driven decline is shifted to higher temperature. A is false (variant is slower at 20–40 °C). C is unsupported: saturating substrate means affinity was not tested. D is false: WT has its maximum rate at 40 °C, so it is still active there.
dx: The variant is slower than WT at 20–40 °C, so its activation energy is not lower at every temperature.
Correct: WT falls after 40 °C while the variant peaks at 50 °C and keeps a rate of 5 at 60 °C.
Substrate was saturating, so affinity was not tested; differences at high temperature reflect stability.
WT has its maximum rate at 40 °C, so it is not yet denatured there.
key.sp: SP1 Concept Explanation · SP4 Representing and Describing Data

cards.title: Question 2
cards.stim: Uptake of two labelled solutes into identical cells was measured over a range of external concentrations. Cells were in the same buffer and the same temperature.

figs.cap: Figure 2. Mean of 3 independent cell batches; error smaller than symbols.

cards.stem: Which statement is most consistent with Figure 2?
opts: A. Solute Y uptake requires ATP hydrolysis by a pump, whereas Solute X uptake is passive and needs no energy input at any concentration.
B. Solute X moves against its concentration gradient, because its uptake rate stops rising at high external concentration while Y’s keeps climbing.
C. Solute X crosses through a limited number of carrier proteins that saturate, whereas Solute Y shows no saturation up to 32 mM.
D. Solute Y enters faster than Solute X at every concentration tested, because its rate is higher at the highest concentration.

key.rationale: A plateau signals a finite number of transport sites (saturation). Y’s rate is proportional to concentration over the tested range, consistent with unmediated or non-saturated passage. A and B infer energy use or gradient direction from kinetics alone. D is false at 1, 2 and 4 mM.
dx: Y’s linear rate says nothing about ATP use; no energy source was manipulated.
A plateau signals saturation, not the direction of the gradient.
Correct: X levels off near 14 while Y is linear to 32 mM.
At 1, 2 and 4 mM X is faster (3, 5.5, 9 vs 1, 2, 4).
key.sp: SP4 Representing and Describing Data · SP6 Argumentation

cards.title: Question 3
cards.stim: Isolated mitochondria are given succinate and ADP. Oligomycin blocks the F₀ channel of ATP synthase. “Uncoupler U” is a lipid-soluble weak acid. Oxygen consumption and ATP made were measured over 5 min.

figs.cap: Figure 3. O₂ values scaled ×0.1 to share an axis. n = 3 independent mitochondrial preparations.

cards.stem: Which explanation for the effect of Uncoupler U is best supported?
opts: A. It inhibits the F₀ channel of ATP synthase, as oligomycin does, so protons cannot return to the matrix and ATP synthesis stops.
B. It blocks electron transfer from the chain to O₂, which collapses the gradient and lowers ATP synthesis as an inhibitor of Complex IV would.
C. It stimulates ATP synthase turnover so ATP is made faster, which draws down the gradient and increases O₂ use to replace it.
D. It makes the inner membrane leak H⁺, so electron transport continues without a gradient large enough to drive ATP synthesis.

key.rationale: Oligomycin lowers both O₂ use (the unrelieved gradient back-pressures the chain) and ATP. U raises O₂ use while ATP falls: the chain is released from back-pressure while the gradient is dissipated. A would lower O₂ use. B contradicts the higher O₂ consumption. C contradicts the ATP data.
dx: Oligomycin lowers O₂ use (4) whereas the uncoupler raises it (18), so the uncoupler does not act on F₀.
Blocking electron transfer would lower O₂ consumption, but it rose.
ATP made fell to 8; it did not rise.
Correct: O₂ use 18 with ATP 8 means the chain runs without a usable gradient.
key.sp: SP1 Concept Explanation · SP4 Representing and Describing Data

cards.title: Question 4
cards.stim: DCPIP is a blue dye that becomes colorless when it accepts electrons. Absorbance at 600 nm was tracked in tubes containing isolated chloroplasts or boiled chloroplasts.
cards.stem: What do the two control tubes together allow the researcher to conclude?
opts: A. DCPIP loses color only when both light and functional chloroplast components are present.
B. Light itself reduces DCPIP; chloroplasts only speed the process.
C. Absence of change in the dark shows chloroplasts do not generate electrons.
D. Boiled chloroplasts prove DCPIP is reduced by the Calvin cycle.

key.rationale: Dark and boiled tubes each remove one requirement and show no change, so decolorization needs light plus intact (heat-labile) components. B is ruled out by the boiled tube. C confuses “needs light” with “makes no electrons.” D: DCPIP intercepts electrons from the light reactions; the Calvin cycle is not tested.
dx: Correct: dark and boiled tubes stay near 0.79 while the lit active tube falls to 0.10.
The boiled-chloroplast tube in light does not change, so light alone does not reduce DCPIP.
The dark tube shows light is needed; it does not show electrons are never made.
DCPIP accepts electrons from the light reactions; the Calvin cycle was not tested.
key.sp: SP3 Questions and Methods · SP4 Representing and Describing Data

cards.title: Question 5
cards.stim: Cultured cells were stained with a DNA dye and analyzed by flow cytometry 24 h after adding Drug D. Cells were binned by DNA content (2N = unreplicated, 4N = replicated).

figs.cap: Figure 5. Single time point; population snapshot.

opts: A. Drug D cells have replicated their DNA but have not divided, and the data cannot separate arrest in G2 from arrest in mitosis.
B. Drug D prevents DNA replication from finishing, so cells pile up with 4N DNA content after a partly completed S phase.
C. Drug D lengthens the cell cycle of every individual cell by 65%, so each cell spends longer in G2/M than before treatment.
D. Drug D causes cells to skip S phase and enter G2 directly, which explains why most treated cells have 4N DNA content.

key.rationale: 65% of treated cells hold 4N DNA, so replication occurred; DNA content cannot distinguish G2 from M. B contradicts the 4N peak. C misreads a population percentage as per-cell timing. D is not supported: S-phase cells remain.
dx: Correct: 65% of treated cells have 4N DNA vs 15% untreated.
Replication occurred (4N cells), and 15% of treated cells are still in S.
A population percentage does not give per-cell durations.
S-phase cells remain (15%), so S phase was not skipped.
key.sp: SP4 Representing and Describing Data · SP6 Argumentation

cards.title: Question 6
cards.stim: A receptor (R) activates Kinase K, which phosphorylates a transcription factor. Pathway output was reported by a fluorescent reporter in cells with WT or mutant R. KI is a specific inhibitor of Kinase K.

figs.cap: Figure 6. Mean ± SD, n = 4 independent cultures.

opts: A. The mutation abolishes ligand binding, which is why output no longer depends on ligand and why the mutant signals as strongly as WT with ligand.
B. KI inhibits the receptor itself rather than Kinase K, because it lowers output to near baseline in both WT and mutant cells.
C. The mutant receptor signals without ligand, and Kinase K is required for the output, but K need not be the only required component.
D. Output in the mutant must rise further as ligand concentration increases, because the mutant receptor still binds ligand and is further activated.

key.rationale: Mutant output ≈ ligand-induced WT output with no ligand (constitutive activity), and KI abolishes it, placing K as required for reporter output. Necessity of K does not exclude other required components. A and D contradict the data; B overreaches (KI target is stated as K).
dx: The mutant gives the same output as WT with ligand; loss of binding would give low output.
KI is the Kinase K inhibitor; inhibition of the receptor itself is not shown.
Correct: mutant ≈ WT + ligand, and KI collapses it to 1.5.
The mutant is already at the WT-with-ligand level without added ligand (9 vs 10).
key.sp: SP6 Argumentation · SP4 Representing and Describing Data

cards.title: Question 7
cards.stim: A lab claims Compound C raises colony counts. They split one bacterial culture into 6 plates (3 control, 3 treated) on a single day.

figs.cap: Figure 7. n = 3 plates per group, all from one culture.

opts: A. Supported: the treated mean is higher than the control mean, and a higher mean colony count is what the claim predicts.
B. Not supported: the overlapping error bars prove that the control and treated groups have identical true mean colony counts.
C. Supported: three plates per group is adequate biological replication, and the colony counts all fall in a reasonable range.
D. Inconclusive: plates from one culture are technical replicates, the 6-colony difference is small relative to the spread, and independent cultures are needed.

key.rationale: Same-culture plates measure pipetting/plating variation, not biological variation, and the 6-colony difference is well within one SD. B overstates (overlap does not prove equality). A ignores variability. C mislabels technical replicates.
dx: 6 colonies is about half an SD, so a higher mean alone is not evidence.
Overlap shows the data are inconclusive, not that the true means are equal.
Plates from one culture are technical, not biological, replicates.
Correct: technical replication, small difference, independent cultures needed.
key.sp: SP5 Statistical Tests and Data Analysis · SP6 Argumentation

cards.title: Question 8
cards.stim: Three hypothetical cuboid cells have identical metabolism per unit volume and take up O₂ only by diffusion across the plasma membrane. Surface area (SA) = 6 × edge²; volume (V) = edge³.
cards.stem: Cell 3 has an SA:V ratio that is what fraction of Cell 1’s, and which change would best restore O₂ supply per unit volume in a cell of that size?
opts: A. One-fourth; a thicker cell wall, which speeds diffusion across the surface.
B. One-fourth; more mitochondria, which increases O₂ supply to the cytoplasm.
C. One-fourth; flattening the cell or folding the membrane into microvilli to add surface area with little added volume.
D. One-half; enlarging the nucleus to coordinate metabolism.

key.rationale: SA:V = 6, 3 and 1.5 for edges 1, 2 and 4 µm, so Cell 3 is one-fourth of Cell 1. Supply scales with SA, demand with V; folding or flattening raises SA/V. A: a wall does not speed diffusion. B raises demand, not supply. D uses the wrong ratio and is unrelated.
dx: A cell wall does not speed diffusion.
More mitochondria raise demand, which worsens the supply problem.
Correct: SA:V = 6, 3, 1.5; folding or flattening adds surface with little volume.
The ratio is one-fourth (1.5/6), not one-half.
key.sp: SP5 Statistical Tests and Data Analysis · SP1 Concept Explanation

cards.title: Question 9
cards.stim: Five dialysis bags, each filled with the same sucrose solution, were placed in beakers of different sucrose concentrations at 25 °C. The tubing is permeable to water but not to sucrose.

figs.cap: Figure 9. Mean of 3 bags per concentration.

opts: A. The bag contents have a solute concentration equivalent to about 0.4 M sucrose, because there was almost no net water movement there.
B. The bag contains 0.8 M sucrose, because mass loss was greatest in the 0.8 M beaker.
C. Water stopped crossing the membrane in the 0.4 M beaker.
D. Sucrose leaves the bag in the 0.8 M beaker, which explains the mass loss.

key.rationale: Net water movement (≈0% change) occurs when the bag and beaker have equal water potential, near 0.4 M. B reverses the logic. C confuses zero net flux with zero movement. D contradicts the stated permeability.
dx: Correct: about 0% change at 0.4 M means no net water movement.
Greatest mass loss shows the beaker is more concentrated than the bag; it does not give the bag’s concentration.
At equal water potential water still crosses in both directions at equal rates.
The tubing is impermeable to sucrose.
key.sp: SP3 Questions and Methods · SP4 Representing and Describing Data

cards.title: Question 10
cards.stim: A small enzyme with four disulfide bonds is denatured in 8 M urea. Activity was then measured after urea was removed by dialysis, with or without prior reduction of disulfide bonds by β-mercaptoethanol (βME).
cards.stem: Which explanation best accounts for all four results?
opts: A. Urea hydrolyzes peptide bonds, so activity can return only if new peptide bonds form once the urea has been removed by dialysis.
B. Urea destroys primary structure, so the activity that returns after removal comes from a small fraction of undamaged enzyme molecules.
C. Sequence alone guarantees complete refolding under all conditions, as the 88% recovery shows, so disulfides play no role in the final structure.
D. Urea disrupts noncovalent interactions that can re-form, but disulfides also stabilize the active structure, so refolding is less efficient without them.

key.rationale: High recovery after urea removal shows the sequence can direct refolding via noncovalent interactions; reduced recovery after βME shows disulfides contribute. A and B misattribute urea’s action to peptide bonds. C ignores the 31% result.
dx: Urea does not break peptide bonds.
Primary structure is intact, which explains the 88% recovery.
Recovery after reduction is only 31%, so disulfides matter.
Correct: 4% in urea, 88% after removal, 31% when disulfides were reduced first.
key.sp: SP1 Concept Explanation · SP6 Argumentation

cards.title: Question 11
cards.stim: Receptor signaling activates Kinases A and B, whose order is unknown, leading to a fluorescent reporter. Cells carried deletions (Δ) or constitutively active (CA) forms. CA kinases need no upstream input.
cards.stem: What is the best-supported order of the pathway components?
opts: A. Receptor → B → A → reporter, because ΔB eliminates output.
B. Receptor → A → B → reporter, because active B bypasses loss of A but active A cannot bypass loss of B.
C. A and B act in separate parallel branches, because each deletion removes output.
D. B is a receptor for the signal, because it can activate the reporter alone.

key.rationale: CA-B restores output without A, so B is downstream; CA-A cannot restore output without B, consistent with A acting through B. A reverses the order. C predicts CA-B would not rescue ΔA. D overreaches.
dx: ΔB abolishes output because B is required, which does not place it upstream; CA-A cannot rescue ΔB.
Correct: CA-B rescues ΔA (9) but CA-A does not rescue ΔB (1.5).
With parallel branches CA-B could not rescue ΔA.
A constitutively active B signals without receptor input; that does not make it the receptor.
key.sp: SP6 Argumentation

cards.title: Question 12
cards.stim: Equal masses (100 g) of water, ethanol and vegetable oil started at 20 °C were heated for 5 min by identical heaters. Oil has no hydrogen bonds between its molecules; ethanol forms fewer per gram than water.
cards.stem: Which explanation best accounts for water’s smaller temperature rise?
opts: A. Water molecules are more massive, so they accelerate more slowly.
B. The covalent O–H bonds of water absorb most of the added heat.
C. Water has weaker intermolecular interactions, so it radiates heat faster.
D. Part of the added energy goes into disrupting hydrogen bonds, so less raises molecular kinetic energy and temperature.

key.rationale: More hydrogen bonds per gram means more heat is absorbed per degree. A is false (water molecules are light). B: heating does not break covalent bonds at these temperatures. C reverses the interaction strength.
dx: Water molecules are less massive than ethanol or oil molecules.
Heating at these temperatures does not break covalent bonds.
Water has stronger, not weaker, intermolecular interactions.
Correct: part of the heat disrupts hydrogen bonds, so the temperature rises less.
key.sp: SP1 Concept Explanation · SP4 Representing and Describing Data

cards.title: Question 13
cards.stim: Initial rates of an enzyme were measured at different substrate concentrations alone (control) and with fixed concentrations of inhibitors P and Q.

figs.cap: Figure 14. Mean of 3 trials; error smaller than symbols.

opts: A. P is competitive: its rates approach control at high substrate, while Q lowers the maximum rate, consistent with binding outside the active site.
B. Q is competitive, because it lowers the rate at every substrate concentration tested and its curve never reaches the control curve.
C. P is noncompetitive, because it lowers the rate by the largest fraction at low substrate and so must reduce the amount of functional enzyme.
D. Both inhibitors are competitive and differ only in potency, because each one lowers the initial rate across the whole range of substrate.

key.rationale: High substrate overcomes a competitive inhibitor (P at 32 mM ≈ 85% of control). Q’s ceiling stays near half the control maximum regardless of substrate, which indicates reduced functioning enzyme. B, C and D misuse “lowers rate” as the criterion.
dx: Correct: P reaches 16 at 32 mM (control 18.8) while Q stays near 9.4.
Lowering the rate at every concentration does not identify competition; Q’s maximum is about halved.
A competitive inhibitor lowers the rate most at low substrate and is overcome at high.
P and Q differ in how substrate affects them, not only in potency.
key.sp: SP1 Concept Explanation · SP4 Representing and Describing Data

cards.title: Question 14
cards.stim: Cells were homogenized and centrifuged as shown. Protein X and two marker enzymes were assayed in each fraction. Microsomes are small closed vesicles that form when membranes break up during homogenization.
opts: A. Protein X is a mitochondrial protein that leaked into other fractions during homogenization, so its pattern reflects damaged organelles.
B. Protein X is in the ER, because the microsomal fraction is made of ER membranes and the ER marker peaks in the same fraction.
C. Protein X is associated with vesicles from internal membranes, but ER, Golgi and other sources cannot be distinguished from these data alone.
D. Protein X is soluble in the cytosol, because it is detected in every fraction and only a minor share pellets with membranes.

key.rationale: 80% of X pellets with microsomes, as does the ER marker, and not with the mitochondrial marker. But microsomes are mixed vesicles, so co-fractionation is suggestive, not proof of ER. D ignores that 93% is in pelleted fractions.
dx: The mitochondrial marker peaks in the mitochondrial fraction (90%) while X is in microsomes (80%).
Microsomes also contain Golgi and plasma-membrane fragments, so they are not only ER.
Correct: co-fractionation with microsomes is suggestive, not proof of ER.
93% of X pellets; only 7% is cytosolic.
key.sp: SP4 Representing and Describing Data · SP6 Argumentation

cards.title: Question 15
cards.stim: Migrating cells were treated with latrunculin (depolymerizes actin filaments), nocodazole (depolymerizes microtubules) or vehicle. Migration speed and the percent of cells with the Golgi positioned next to the nucleus were measured.

figs.cap: Figure 16. n = 150 cells per bar from 3 independent experiments.

opts: A. Both filament types contribute about equally to migration and to Golgi position, because each drug changed both measurements.
B. Actin is required for most migration but not Golgi positioning; microtubules are required for Golgi positioning but add little to speed.
C. Microtubules drive cell migration, because nocodazole lowers speed, and actin only maintains the position of the Golgi near the nucleus.
D. Latrunculin disrupts Golgi position because it lowers speed, so loss of movement is what moves the Golgi away from the nucleus.

key.rationale: Latrunculin: speed 30→5, Golgi 90→85. Nocodazole: speed 30→24, Golgi 90→20. C overweights a modest reduction; D infers causation across measures.
dx: The two drugs affect the two measures very differently.
Correct: latrunculin 30→5 speed, 90→85 Golgi; nocodazole 30→24 speed, 90→20 Golgi.
Nocodazole lowers speed only modestly (30→24).
Latrunculin barely changes Golgi position (90→85); the two measures are not causally linked here.
key.sp: SP6 Argumentation · SP3 Questions and Methods

cards.title: Question 16
cards.stim: Oxygen consumption rate (OCR) of cells was measured after sequential additions: oligomycin (blocks ATP synthase), FCCP (drives respiration to its maximum rate), and rotenone + antimycin A (block the chain; residual is non-mitochondrial). ATP-linked respiration = basal − oligomycin value. Spare capacity = FCCP − basal.
opts: A. ATP-linked 30; spare capacity 80
B. ATP-linked 70; spare capacity 150
C. ATP-linked 95; spare capacity 80
D. ATP-linked 70; spare capacity 80

key.rationale: ATP-linked = 100 − 30 = 70. Spare = 180 − 100 = 80. A uses the oligomycin value; B subtracts oligomycin from FCCP; C subtracts the non-mitochondrial value.
dx: 30 is the oligomycin-insensitive value, not ATP-linked respiration.
150 subtracts oligomycin from FCCP instead of basal.
95 subtracts the non-mitochondrial value.
key.sp: SP5 Statistical Tests and Data Analysis · SP4 Representing and Describing Data

cards.title: Question 17
cards.stim: Yeast cultures grown on glucose were run as shown. Glucose uptake, ethanol production and O₂ use were measured.
cards.stem: Why is glucose consumption higher in Culture 2?
opts: A. Ethanol production consumes ATP, so more glucose must be broken down in the sealed culture to pay for making the ethanol.
B. Fermentation yields more ATP per glucose than respiration does, so the sealed culture takes up more glucose to make more ATP.
C. Fermentation yields far less ATP per glucose, so more glucose is processed to meet demand; ethanol formation regenerates NAD⁺ so glycolysis continues.
D. Without O₂, glycolysis stops and glucose is instead used by the citric acid cycle, which explains the higher glucose consumption.

key.rationale: Glycolysis nets 2 ATP per glucose versus roughly 30 with oxidative phosphorylation. A and B reverse the energetics. D is wrong: the citric acid cycle needs the O₂-dependent chain to regenerate NAD⁺.
dx: Fermentation does not consume ATP overall; glycolysis nets 2 ATP.
Fermentation yields about 2 ATP per glucose vs about 30 with respiration.
Correct: low ATP yield forces more glucose use, and ethanol formation regenerates NAD⁺.
Glycolysis continues without O₂; the citric acid cycle needs the O₂-dependent chain.
key.sp: SP1 Concept Explanation · SP4 Representing and Describing Data

cards.title: Question 18
cards.stim: Illuminated algae supplied with CO₂ were suddenly darkened at 0 s. Levels of 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PGA) and ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP) were measured.
opts: A. Rubisco requires light directly, so carbon fixation halts at once and RuBP is no longer consumed after the lamp is switched off.
B. ATP and NADPH stop, so 3-PGA is not reduced and RuBP is not regenerated, while rubisco keeps using remaining RuBP to make 3-PGA.
C. CO₂ cannot enter the cells in darkness, so less 3-PGA is made from RuBP and the 3-PGA level falls after the lamp is switched off.
D. In darkness 3-PGA is converted back to RuBP faster than before, so RuBP rises as the 3-PGA is used up.

key.rationale: Fixation of CO₂ onto RuBP continues briefly (RuBP falls, 3-PGA rises) but reduction and regeneration need ATP/NADPH. A, C and D contradict the data directions.
dx: RuBP falls because rubisco keeps using it; rubisco does not need light directly.
Correct: 3-PGA 100→165 while RuBP 100→10.
3-PGA rose rather than fell.
RuBP fell while 3-PGA rose, the opposite of this option.
key.sp: SP6 Argumentation · SP1 Concept Explanation

cards.title: Question 19
cards.stim: Cells were given a ligand at time 0 and cAMP was measured, with or without a phosphodiesterase (PDE) inhibitor.
opts: A. PDE helps terminate the signal by degrading cAMP; the initial rise does not require PDE.
B. The inhibitor increases adenylyl cyclase activity.
C. The decline in control cells proves the ligand was removed from the medium.
D. PDE is needed for the initial rise in cAMP.

key.rationale: Rise is identical through 2 min; only the decline differs. B contradicts the equal early rise. C is unsupported. D is contradicted.
dx: Correct: the rise is identical through 2 min; only the decline differs.
The early rise is the same, so synthesis rate is unchanged.
Ligand clearance was not measured; degradation or feedback could explain the decline.
The initial rise is the same when PDE is inhibited.
key.sp: SP1 Concept Explanation · SP4 Representing and Describing Data

cards.title: Question 20
cards.stim: WT cells and cells lacking checkpoint protein C were irradiated, and the percent in G1 was measured 24 h later. Measured DNA damage immediately after irradiation was equal in both cell types.
cards.stem: Which prediction is best supported if ΔC cells are repeatedly irradiated?
opts: A. ΔC cells sustain less DNA damage and so need no arrest.
B. ΔC cells arrest in G2 instead, so they accumulate no mutations.
C. ΔC cells enter S phase with damaged DNA, so mutations should accumulate faster than in WT.
D. ΔC cells undergo more apoptosis than WT.

key.rationale: WT increases G1 fraction (arrest); ΔC does not despite equal damage, so ΔC proceeds through the cycle. A contradicts the stem; B and D are unsupported by the data.
dx: Damage was equal immediately after irradiation.
G2 arrest was not measured, and arrested cells would not accumulate mutations in this way.
Correct: no G1 increase despite equal damage.
Apoptosis was not measured.
key.sp: SP6 Argumentation

cards.title: Question 21
cards.stim: Synthetic vesicles were built with a pure lipid bilayer or with the same bilayer plus a purified membrane protein, and loaded with no solute. External solutes S (hydrophilic) and L (lipid-soluble) were added at equal concentration, and initial uptake rates were measured (no ATP in the system). Simulations of the two membrane designs are shown above.

figs.cap: Figure 22. Mean ± SD, n = 4 vesicle preparations.

opts: A. S is moved by active transport, because the protein increases its uptake rate about twenty-fold compared with the pure bilayer.
B. S crosses through the protein by facilitated diffusion down its gradient, whereas L crosses the lipid bilayer and is unaffected by the protein.
C. L is carried by the protein, because its uptake rate is the highest of all the measurements shown for these vesicles.
D. At equilibrium individual S and L molecules stop crossing the membrane, so net and gross movement are both zero once concentrations match.

key.rationale: No ATP is supplied, so S uptake that depends on the protein is passive (facilitated). L is already fast in the pure bilayer and is unchanged, so it does not need the protein. At equilibrium crossings continue equally in both directions (visible in the simulation).
dx: Mistakes a protein-dependent rate increase for ATP use; no ATP was supplied, so transport is passive.
Correct: the protein raises S about 20-fold (facilitated, down its gradient) while L stays 30→31.
L is already fast without the protein, which adds nothing.
At equilibrium crossings continue equally in both directions.
key.sp: SP1 Concept Explanation · SP4 Representing and Describing Data

cards.title: Question 22
cards.stim: A GFP-tagged membrane-associated protein (green) was imaged with a nuclear DNA dye (red) in control cells, cells treated 1 h with Drug M, and cells 1 h after Drug M washout. Fluorescence intensity was quantified.

figs.cap: Figure 23. Mean ± SD, n = 60 cells per bar, 3 experiments.

opts: A. Drug M triggers degradation of the protein, which is why membrane fluorescence is lost and why total fluorescence per cell would be expected to fall.
B. Drug M irreversibly misfolds the protein, so it is trapped in the cytoplasm and cannot return to the membrane after the drug is removed.
C. Drug M blocks synthesis of new protein, so the existing membrane pool is gradually used up and total GFP in each cell declines.
D. Drug M reversibly reduces membrane association without changing total protein, though these data do not establish the mechanism.

key.rationale: Total GFP is constant (no degradation or synthesis block) and the ratio recovers on washout (reversible). The mechanism (for example lipid modification or binding partner) is not tested.
dx: Total GFP stays near 100%, so no degradation.
The ratio recovers after washout (4.0), so the effect is reversible.
Total GFP is unchanged, so synthesis is not blocked.
Correct: ratio 4.5→0.9→4.0 with constant total GFP.
key.sp: SP4 Representing and Describing Data · SP6 Argumentation

cards.title: Question 23
cards.stim: Membrane fluidity was measured by fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP). A shorter recovery half-time indicates faster lateral diffusion of lipids. Liposomes contained phospholipids with only saturated tails or with one unsaturated (cis) tail.
cards.stem: Which explanation best accounts for the difference at 10 °C?
opts: A. The cis double bond creates a kink that prevents tight packing, so the bilayer stays fluid at low temperature.
B. Saturated tails pack loosely and leave gaps between lipids, which is why they diffuse more slowly than unsaturated tails at 10 °C.
C. Temperature does not affect lateral diffusion in bilayers, so the differences at 10 °C reflect only the headgroup, not the tails.
D. Unsaturated tails form covalent crosslinks between the two leaflets, which holds lipids in place and speeds recovery after bleaching.

key.rationale: Kinked tails increase spacing and lower the packing density. Saturated tails pack tightly and slow at low T; this difference shrinks as temperature rises.
dx: Correct: the kink lowers packing density; half-time 30 s vs 90 s at 10 °C.
Reverses the packing relationship.
Both series speed up with temperature.
Cis double bonds create kinks; they are not crosslinks.
key.sp: SP1 Concept Explanation · SP4 Representing and Describing Data

cards.title: Question 24
cards.stim: Researchers measured leaf nitrogen and photosynthetic rate in 7 field plots, with no manipulation. Sunnier plots also had wetter soil.
cards.stem: What is the most defensible conclusion and follow-up?
opts: A. Nitrogen causes higher photosynthesis, because the association across the seven plots is strong and rises steadily with leaf nitrogen.
B. Photosynthesis causes greater nitrogen uptake, because the photosynthetic rate rises together with leaf nitrogen in every plot measured.
C. The association is observational and confounded by light and water; randomly assigned fertilizer treatments with controls would test causation.
D. The relationship plateaus at high nitrogen, so adding more nitrogen beyond about 3 g/m² would be expected to give no extra benefit.

key.rationale: Strong correlation does not establish direction or cause when light and moisture covary with both variables. A manipulative experiment isolates nitrogen. D is not shown (the data are still rising).
dx: Strong correlation alone cannot show cause; light and water covary.
Direction cannot be inferred from observation.
Correct: confounded, observational; randomized fertilizer plots with controls would test cause.
Rates are still rising at the highest nitrogen; no plateau is shown.
key.sp: SP6 Argumentation · SP3 Questions and Methods

cards.title: Question 25
cards.stim: Two genotypes were measured in n = 4 independent plants each. The error bars show the standard error of the mean (SEM); the sample SD in each group is 2.0.
opts: A. The genotypes differ, because the means differ by 1.2 cm and the error bar on each mean is only 1.0 cm in length.
B. Since SEM = SD/√n = 1.0, intervals of at least ±2 SEM overlap heavily, so the data do not support a difference; more replicates would narrow them.
C. The overlapping error bars prove that the true means of the two genotypes are identical, so no further replicates could reveal a difference.
D. The bars show SD = 1.0, so the plants within each group are tightly clustered and the 1.2 cm difference between groups is large relative to it.

key.rationale: Even ±2 SEM intervals (2.1–6.1 and 3.3–7.3) overlap substantially, and the t-based 95% interval for n = 4 (about ±3.2) is wider still. Absence of support is not proof of equality (C). The bars are SEM, not SD (D).
dx: Ignores SEM = 1.0 and n = 4; 1.2 cm is about 1 SEM.
Correct: SEM = 2.0/√4 = 1.0; ±2 SEM intervals overlap heavily.
Overlap shows inconclusiveness, not equality.
The bars are SEM, not SD (SD = 2.0).
key.unit: Unit 0 · Error bars and sample size
key.sp: SP5 Statistical Tests and Data Analysis · SP6 Argumentation

cards.title: Question 26
cards.stim: Glutamine synthesis (glutamate + NH₄⁺ → glutamine) alone has ΔG = +14 kJ/mol. ATP hydrolysis has ΔG = −30.5 kJ/mol. A cell couples the two through a phosphorylated intermediate.

figs.cap: Figure 27. Standard values for this hypothetical system.

opts: A. Glutamine synthesis proceeds on its own, because ATP hydrolysis is exergonic and any energy released in the cell can be used by it.
B. Coupling lowers the activation energy of glutamine synthesis, which is what makes its ΔG negative in the presence of ATP.
C. ATP supplies the carbon atoms for glutamine, which is why the reaction is favorable only when ATP is present at high concentration.
D. The overall ΔG of −16.5 kJ/mol makes the coupled process favorable, but ΔG does not predict how fast it proceeds.

key.rationale: +14 + (−30.5) = −16.5. Enzymes lower activation energy but do not change ΔG (B). Thermodynamic favorability says nothing about rate.
dx: Exergonic ATP hydrolysis alone does not drive an unlinked reaction.
Enzymes lower activation energy but cannot change ΔG.
ATP supplies phosphate and energy, not carbon.
Correct: +14 − 30.5 = −16.5 kJ/mol; ΔG says nothing about rate.
key.sp: SP1 Concept Explanation · SP5 Statistical Tests and Data Analysis

cards.title: Question 27
cards.stim: Two unknown cell types were stained with a DNA dye (red) and a dye that binds membranes of the nuclear envelope and endoplasmic reticulum (green).
opts: A. In Cell type 1 the DNA is not enclosed by a stained nuclear envelope, consistent with a prokaryote; in Cell type 2 the DNA sits inside a membrane.
B. Cell type 1 has no DNA, because its red signal is spread through the cytoplasm rather than concentrated in a single compact organelle.
C. Cell type 2 is a prokaryote, because the green ring around its DNA is a cell wall that holds the chromosome in place inside the cell.
D. Size alone proves that Cell type 1 is a prokaryote, because its small rod-shaped cells are far smaller than those of Cell type 2.

key.rationale: The stain locates DNA relative to internal membranes. A single stain cannot prove the absence of all organelles, but the contrast with Cell type 2 is the evidence. B and D ignore the data; C misreads the dye.
dx: Correct: the DNA is not enclosed by a stained membrane compartment in type 1; type 2 has a nuclear envelope ring.
Type 1 has a red DNA signal.
The green dye labels envelope and ER membranes, not cell wall.
Size is suggestive, not proof.
key.sp: SP4 Representing and Describing Data · SP1 Concept Explanation

cards.title: Question 28
cards.stim: Synchronized cells were released at 0 h. Cells expressed normal cyclin B (WT) or a degradation-resistant cyclin B (mutant). Cyclin B levels and the mitotic index (% of cells in mitosis) were measured.
opts: A. Cyclin B degradation is required for mitotic entry, since mutant cells with stable cyclin B take much longer to enter mitosis than WT cells.
B. Cyclin B is not needed for mitosis, because mutant cells with an altered form of cyclin B still reach a high mitotic index.
C. Cells with non-degradable cyclin B enter mitosis normally but cannot complete exit, so degradation is needed to leave mitosis.
D. The mutant reduces CDK activity at 6 h, which is why its cells accumulate in mitosis instead of progressing back to interphase.

key.rationale: Cyclin B rises equally through 6 h and mitotic entry occurs (index reaches 35% at 6 h and keeps climbing), but cells accumulate in mitosis when cyclin B stays high.
dx: Cyclin B rises to the same level before entry; degradation matters for exit.
Cyclin B peaks at mitosis in WT, so it is involved.
Correct: mutant mitotic index climbs to 75% while cyclin B stays high.
CDK activity was not measured.
key.sp: SP6 Argumentation · SP4 Representing and Describing Data

cards.title: Question 29
cards.stim: A transcription factor fused to GFP (green) was imaged with a DNA dye (red). Ligand was added at 0 min; one group received a Kinase K inhibitor 30 min earlier.

figs.cap: Figure 29. Mean ± SD, n = 50 cells per bar.

opts: A. The inhibitor blocks ligand binding to its receptor, which is why the transcription factor fails to accumulate in the nucleus after ligand addition.
B. Kinase K activity is required for ligand-induced nuclear accumulation; the data do not show that K phosphorylates the factor or that it binds DNA.
C. The inhibitor degrades the transcription factor in the cytosol, which is why no nuclear signal appears when ligand is added to treated cells.
D. The ligand directly imports the transcription factor into the nucleus, so a kinase is not needed for the change in localization.

key.rationale: The inhibitor abolishes the ligand-induced shift, so K activity is needed. Direct phosphorylation, receptor binding or DNA binding are not measured.
dx: Ligand binding was not tested; the inhibitor acts on nuclear accumulation.
Correct: ratio 3.1→0.4 with inhibitor.
No loss of total GFP is shown; the factor redistributes.
Direct import by the ligand is not shown; kinase K is required.
key.sp: SP4 Representing and Describing Data · SP6 Argumentation

cards.title: Question 30
cards.stim: Cells expressing a mutant mitochondrial carrier were stained with a dye whose mitochondrial fluorescence increases with membrane potential (red). An ATP biosensor and an energy-stress reporter (a.u.) were also measured.
cards.stem: Which interpretation is best supported, and what would test it?
opts: A. The mutation raises the proton gradient across the inner membrane, so ATP synthesis is overdriven and ATP falls through increased use.
B. The rise in the stress reporter shows that the mutant has more ATP than WT, because the reporter responds to energy-replete cells.
C. Lower ATP caused the loss of membrane potential, because the mutant mitochondria cannot hold a gradient without ATP-dependent proton pumping.
D. The carrier mutation lowers the gradient and ATP, consistent with an ATP-sensing reporter; restoring ATP in the mutant would test causation.

key.rationale: Lower dye signal = lower membrane potential, lower ATP and higher stress reporter are all consistent, but these are co-measured endpoints, so ordering is not proven. A and B contradict the data; C reverses the usual dependence of ATP synthesis on the gradient.
dx: Dye signal is lower, so potential is lower, not higher.
A higher stress reporter indicates less ATP.
The dependence runs the other way: potential drives ATP synthesis.
Correct: all measures agree, but ordering needs a rescue experiment.
key.sp: SP6 Argumentation · SP1 Concept Explanation

cards.title: Question B1
cards.stim: Yeast cells lacking Complex IV cannot make ATP by oxidative phosphorylation. They are engineered to express “LDP,” a light-driven pump that moves H⁺ from the matrix into the intermembrane space and uses no electrons from the respiratory chain. ATP was measured in isolated mitochondria with substrate and ADP.

figs.cap: Figure 8. Mean ± SD, n = 3 independent preparations.

opts: A. LDP passes electrons to oxygen and so replaces Complex IV, which is why ATP returns in the light in cells that lack Complex IV.
B. A H⁺ gradient made without respiratory-chain electron flow can drive ATP synthase here, and the ATP made depends on an intact membrane and ATP synthase.
C. Light stimulates substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis, so the ATP seen in the light comes from enhanced glycolytic flux rather than from a gradient.
D. Complex IV is dispensable for ATP production in WT cells, because the pump restores ATP to near-WT levels with no respiratory-chain contribution.

key.rationale: Light + LDP restores ATP to near-WT only when LDP is present; the uncoupler (dissipates gradient) and oligomycin (blocks F₀) each abolish it. A is contrary to the stated design. C fails because substrate-level ATP would not be abolished by uncoupler or oligomycin. D extrapolates: ΔIV shows Complex IV loss prevents ATP, and LDP bypasses via the gradient, not that IV is dispensable.
dx: LDP uses no respiratory-chain electrons.
Correct: light + LDP restores ATP; uncoupler and oligomycin abolish it.
Substrate-level ATP would not be abolished by uncoupler or oligomycin.
Extrapolates: IV loss removes ATP; the pump bypasses via the gradient.
key.sp: SP1 Concept Explanation · SP6 Argumentation

cards.title: Question B2
cards.stim: Flow cytometry showed that Drug E raises the fraction of 4N cells from 15% to 40%. Two models: (M1) Drug E lengthens G2 modestly in every cell; (M2) Drug E arrests a subpopulation in G2 while the rest progress normally. Time-lapse imaging tracked 200 cells per group for 24 h and scored G2 duration.

figs.cap: Figure 12. 200 cells per group from 2 independent cultures.

cards.stem: Which model is best supported by the time-lapse data?
opts: A. M1: the whole distribution shifts to longer durations, so every cell is slowed modestly and the rise in 4N cells reflects uniform lengthening of G2.
B. M2 is excluded because some drug-treated cells still divide within 4–8 h, which shows that no subpopulation is arrested by Drug E.
C. M2: about 28% of cells are arrested in G2 while the rest progress as in control, so the drug acts on a subpopulation rather than on every cell.
D. Drug E blocks DNA replication in 28% of cells, so those cells never reach 4N and are scored as still in G2 at 24 h.

key.rationale: The main peak (4–8 h) resembles control and 28% of drug-treated cells remain in G2 beyond 20 h: a distinct arrested subpopulation, not a uniform shift. A predicts the whole distribution moves; B misreads the cells that still divide; D contradicts cells being in G2 (after replication).
dx: The distribution is not uniformly shifted; 28% exceed 20 h.
Some dividing cells do not exclude partial arrest.
Correct: main peak resembles control plus a 28% arrested group; flow alone could not separate the models.
G2 cells have already replicated DNA.
key.sp: SP6 Argumentation · SP4 Representing and Describing Data

cards.title: Question B3
cards.stim: A tetrameric enzyme shows a sigmoidal rate curve. Adding activator A makes the curve hyperbolic. A subunit-interface mutant (Mut) has a hyperbolic curve on its own and does not respond to A. The same enzyme concentration was used throughout.

figs.cap: Figure 31. Mean of 3 trials; error smaller than symbols.

cards.stem: Which interpretation accounts for all four curves?
opts: A. The mutation raises Vmax, because Mut is faster than WT at low substrate, so the interface change must increase the catalytic rate of each subunit.
B. Activator A raises the catalytic rate of every enzyme molecule, because it increases the rate at low substrate where WT is slowest.
C. Mut behaves like activator-bound WT: it is locked in a high-affinity form so A adds nothing, and WT’s sigmoidal shape reflects subunit cooperativity.
D. A binds the active site and is displaced by substrate at high concentration, which is why all four curves converge at the same maximum rate.

key.rationale: All four curves plateau near 18.5, so Vmax is unchanged (A, B). A only changes how readily the enzyme reaches its high-affinity state. Mut ≈ WT + A, and A adds nothing to Mut. D fails because a displaced active-site binder would not activate.
dx: Vmax is about 18.5 in all four curves.
At saturation all rates are equal, so kcat is unchanged.
Correct: Mut ≈ WT + A, and A adds nothing to Mut.
A displaced competitor would inhibit, not activate.
key.sp: SP6 Argumentation · SP4 Representing and Describing Data

cards.title: Question B4
cards.stim: Glucose uptake into cells was measured over 20 min. Ouabain blocks the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase, and intracellular [Na⁺] measured in parallel rose from 10 mM (0 min) to 18, 35 and 80 mM at 5, 10 and 20 min. In a third group, extracellular Na⁺ was replaced by choline.
opts: A. Glucose entry depends on the Na⁺ gradient, and ouabain acts indirectly because the gradient collapses gradually once the pump is blocked.
B. Ouabain binds the glucose transporter itself, but slowly, so its inhibition takes minutes to develop and mimics the rise in intracellular Na⁺.
C. Glucose enters by facilitated diffusion down its own gradient, and Na⁺ has an unrelated, minor effect on the transporter’s activity.
D. The transporter hydrolyzes ATP directly, and ouabain lowers ATP within minutes, which gradually inactivates the glucose transporter.

key.rationale: Na⁺-free medium nearly abolishes uptake at once, so Na⁺ is required. Ouabain’s effect tracks the slow loss of the Na⁺ gradient (intracellular Na⁺ rising). B predicts an immediate effect size set by binding, not by [Na⁺]. C is contradicted by 8%. D is unsupported; ouabain does not deplete ATP on this time scale.
dx: Correct: Na⁺-free medium abolishes uptake; ouabain tracks the collapse of the Na⁺ gradient.
Slow binding would not follow intracellular Na⁺.
Na⁺-free medium gives 8% uptake.
Ouabain does not deplete ATP on this timescale.
key.sp: SP6 Argumentation · SP4 Representing and Describing Data

cards.title: Question B5
cards.stim: A mutant plant lacks cyclic electron flow around Photosystem I (which pumps H⁺ but makes no NADPH or O₂). Both plants were measured in high light with normal CO₂. The Calvin cycle uses ATP and NADPH in a 3:2 ratio.
cards.stem: Which explanation is best supported, and what predicts it?
opts: A. Photosystem II is damaged in the mutant, which lowers NADPH production and so limits CO₂ fixation through reduced reducing power.
B. Rubisco is inactive in the mutant, so the Calvin cycle consumes less NADPH and ATP and the products of the light reactions accumulate.
C. The mutant overproduces ATP, which feeds back to inhibit the Calvin cycle, so fixation falls while NADPH is left unused.
D. Linear flow alone supplies too little ATP relative to NADPH, so NADPH accumulates while ATP limits fixation; supplying extra ATP would raise fixation.

key.rationale: High NADPH reduction with low ATP/ADP and reduced fixation indicates ATP limitation. A contradicts the high NADPH fraction. B would leave ATP/ADP high. C contradicts the low ATP/ADP ratio.
dx: NADPH is already highly reduced (90%).
Inactive rubisco would raise ATP/ADP.
ATP/ADP is low (1.0).
Correct: ATP-limited with NADPH accumulating.
key.sp: SP6 Argumentation · SP1 Concept Explanation

cards.title: Question B6
cards.stim: Receptor occupancy by ligand was measured by radioligand binding (Kd = 50 nM). A cellular response was measured in control cells and in cells in which about 80% of receptors were irreversibly inactivated.
opts: A. The response is proportional to receptor occupancy at every ligand concentration, so occupancy alone sets the size of the cellular response.
B. Downstream amplification gives a half-maximal response at low occupancy; fewer receptors raise the ligand needed without lowering the maximum, which is set downstream.
C. Receptor loss lowers the maximum response, which proves the response is receptor-limited rather than limited by a downstream component.
D. The Kd is 1 nM, since half-maximal response occurs at 1 nM, so the receptor binds ligand with higher affinity than the binding data suggest.

key.rationale: Control half-max response occurs at about 1 nM, where only about 2% of receptors are occupied. After losing 80% of receptors the curve shifts right (half-max near 10 nM) but reaches the same maximum. C reverses this. D confuses EC₅₀ with Kd (50 nM here).
dx: Half-maximal response occurs at 2% occupancy.
Correct: amplification; the curve shifts right with the same maximum.
The maximum is unchanged (99–100%).
EC₅₀ (1 nM) is not Kd (50 nM).
key.sp: SP1 Concept Explanation · SP4 Representing and Describing Data

cards.title: Question B7
cards.stim: Quiescent cells were given growth factor (GF) for different durations and then GF was removed. The percent of cells that entered S phase by 24 h was measured. A second group also received cycloheximide (blocks protein synthesis) during the pulse.

figs.cap: Figure 35. Population measurement, n = 500 cells per point.

opts: A. Growth factor triggers S entry directly within 2 h of exposure, so the length of the pulse is irrelevant to whether cells commit to dividing.
B. Protein synthesis is dispensable for commitment, as shown by the cycloheximide group, so growth factor acts through existing proteins only.
C. Every individual cell needs exactly 6 h of growth factor, as shown by the 70% value at 6 h, so all cells share one commitment time.
D. Commitment needs protein made during growth-factor exposure, and after about 8 h of exposure most cells no longer need the factor to enter S phase.

key.rationale: Cycloheximide holds S entry at about 3% for every pulse, so protein made during exposure is needed. Pulses of 8–12 h give 90–95%, close to continuous growth factor (95%), so cells past commitment no longer need it. A is contradicted by low S entry after short pulses, B by the cycloheximide group, and C overreads one percentage as a per-cell requirement.
dx: Short pulses give little S entry.
Cycloheximide abolishes commitment, so protein is needed.
Population percentages cannot show an exact per-cell time.
Correct: protein-dependent, and population data cannot show all-or-none.
key.sp: SP6 Argumentation

cards.title: Question B8
cards.stim: Isolated thylakoid vesicles were equilibrated in the dark, mixed into a new buffer containing ADP and Pᵢ, and ATP was measured after 15 s. Nigericin exchanges H⁺ for K⁺ across membranes. DCMU blocks Photosystem II. The inside/outside pH of the vesicles is given for each condition.
cards.stem: Which statement best identifies what the nigericin condition adds beyond the equal-pH (inside 8 → outside 8) condition?
opts: A. It repeats every step of the 100% condition but dissipates the pH difference, so the loss of ATP can be attributed to the gradient and not to the pH 4 pre-equilibration or the mixing step.
B. It shows that ATP synthase is inhibited by high pH, because ATP falls to 6% in a medium that is at pH 8 outside the vesicles.
C. It shows that a pH difference is not required, because nigericin exchanges H⁺ for K⁺ and the resulting K⁺ gradient drives ATP synthesis instead.
D. It repeats the DCMU result, because both treatments remove electron flow, so both confirm that ATP depends on light-driven electron transport.

key.rationale: Nigericin keeps every step identical to the 100% condition but dissipates the pH difference, so the drop to 6% is due to the gradient and not to pre-equilibration at pH 4, the mixing step or the buffers; the equal-pH condition also changes the pre-equilibration. B: pH 8 outside is also present in the 100% condition. C: removing the H⁺ gradient abolishes ATP. D: DCMU leaves ATP at 98%, so electron flow is not required.
dx: Correct: only the acidic-inside condition makes ATP; DCMU is irrelevant.
DCMU (no PSII flow) still gives ATP.
Reversed and equal-pH conditions give about zero.
Nigericin dissipates the gradient; the synthase is intact.
key.sp: SP3 Questions and Methods · SP6 Argumentation

cards.title: Question B9
cards.stim: Spherical cell clusters of different radii consume O₂ at the same rate per volume. Steady-state O₂ was measured at the center as a percent of surface level. For a sphere with uniform consumption, the drop from surface to center is proportional to (radius)² and to the consumption rate per volume.

figs.cap: Figure 37. Mean ± SD, n = 8 clusters per radius.

cards.stem: About what radius first gives an anoxic center, and what radius would do so if consumption per volume were halved?
opts: A. About 220 µm; about 440 µm.
B. About 220 µm; about 310 µm.
C. About 300 µm; about 600 µm.
D. About 150 µm; about 210 µm.

key.rationale: A 20% drop at 100 µm scales as r², so the drop is 100% at 100·√5 ≈ 224 µm (checks: 150 µm → 45% drop; 200 µm → 80%, observed 75%, within error). Halving the rate halves the drop at any radius, so the radius for a full drop rises by √2: about 316 µm. A uses a linear scaling; C and D ignore the data.
dx: 440 µm assumes linear, not r², scaling.
Correct: 100√5 ≈ 224 µm, then ×√2 ≈ 316 µm.
300 µm is already anoxic in the data.
At 150 µm the center is still at 55%.
key.sp: SP5 Statistical Tests and Data Analysis · SP6 Argumentation

cards.title: Question B10
cards.stim: Cells expressing a constitutively active kinase K (CA-K) were compared with WT. Basal measurements are shown with the same cells after adding FCCP (which drives respiration to its maximum rate). A third group had a specific K inhibitor (KI).
opts: A. CA-K damages the electron transport chain, so respiration is limited by the chain and the membrane potential falls along with ATP production.
B. CA-K increases proton leak across the inner membrane, so the chain runs faster to compensate and ATP synthesis is diverted from phosphorylation.
C. CA-K restricts H⁺ flow through ATP synthase, raising the gradient and back-pressuring an intact chain; the K inhibitor reverses it.
D. CA-K limits substrate supply to the chain, so less NADH reaches Complex I and ATP, O₂ use and the membrane potential all decrease.

key.rationale: Low ATP and O₂ use with a higher potential means reduced proton flux through ATP synthase. FCCP restores maximal O₂ use (about 195%), so the chain is intact (A). A leak would raise O₂ use and lower potential (B). Limited substrate would lower potential and FCCP-stimulated respiration (D). KI reversing it links the effect to K activity.
dx: FCCP restores near-maximal O₂ use (195%).
A leak would raise O₂ use and lower potential.
Correct: high potential with low O₂ and ATP, an intact chain, and reversal by KI.
Limited substrate would lower potential and FCCP-O₂ use.
key.sp: SP6 Argumentation · SP4 Representing and Describing Data

cards.title: FRQ 1 (long)
cards.stim:
Baker’s yeast (WT) and a mutant lacking Complex III were grown on glucose at 30 °C. Both strains also carry a hypothetical alternative oxidase (AOX) that passes electrons from the quinone pool (Q) directly to O₂ without proton pumping at Complexes III or IV. Rates are mean ± SD, n = 3 cultures.

WTMutant
O₂ consumption (µmol/min/g)12.0 ± 0.81.5 ± 0.3
Ethanol production (µmol/min/g)0.1 ± 0.0514.0 ± 1.1
Growth on glucose (doublings/h)0.40 ± 0.020.18 ± 0.02
Figure 1. Electron path in each strain. Dashed = pathway through the AOX branch.
Figure 2. Oxygen remaining in a sealed chamber. AOX inhibitor added at 0 min where shown.

subs.html: (a) Calculate the percent change in O₂ consumption of the mutant relative to WT.
(b) Explain how loss of Complex III leads to the change in ethanol production.

key.rationale: electrons cannot pass through the chain, so NADH is not reoxidized to NAD⁺ by it (1); NAD⁺ for glycolysis is regenerated by fermenting pyruvate to ethanol (1).

subs.html: (c) A student claims, “Because the mutant still consumes O₂, Complex III must be partly functional.” Evaluate this claim using Figure 2, and identify one further measurement that would test Complex III activity directly.

key.rationale: claim not supported: with the AOX inhibitor, O₂ use falls to near zero, so residual use goes through AOX, not Complex III (1); direct test: antimycin A sensitivity of O₂ use, or measure cytochrome c reduction by quinol/Complex III assay (1).

subs.html: (d) Predict the mutant’s growth on glycerol (a non-fermentable carbon source) relative to glucose, and justify.

key.rationale: much slower than on glucose, since glycerol requires oxidative phosphorylation and the mutant’s chain pumps few protons.

subs.html: (e) Justify the claim that the mutant makes most of its ATP by glycolysis.

key.rationale: low O₂ use, high ethanol and reduced growth indicate little oxidative phosphorylation.

subs.html: (f) A reviewer proposes that slow growth is caused by ethanol toxicity, not low ATP yield. Describe one experiment that could discriminate between these explanations and state the result that would support the reviewer.

key.rationale: grow WT with added ethanol (matching the mutant’s level) or the mutant with ethanol removed; if WT slows with ethanol, or the mutant recovers when ethanol is removed, the reviewer is supported.Common errors: saying fermentation yields ATP from ethanol; treating any O₂ use as Complex III activity.

subs.html: (g) Draw [2 pts]. Draw and label the respiratory chain of the mutant on the pad: show where electron flow stops, the alternative route to O₂, and which steps still pump protons.

key.rationale: 1 pt: order NADH → Complex I → Q, with the block marked at Complex III so electrons cannot reach Complex IV; 1 pt: AOX branch from Q to O₂ drawn, with H⁺ pumping shown at Complex I only (not at III or IV).NADHIQIIIcyt cIVO₂AOX: no H⁺ pumpedH⁺ pumped

cards.title: FRQ 2 (long)
cards.stim:
A hypothetical receptor R makes the second messenger M when it binds ligand L. A FRET biosensor reported intracellular [M] (µM) 5 min after adding L, in 3 independent cultures per dose.

[L] (nM)01101001000
Culture 10.10.72.77.27.5
Culture 20.20.93.17.88.2
Culture 30.31.13.58.48.9

Additional observations: (i) at 1000 nM L plus a cell-permeable activator of the enzyme that makes M, [M] = 14.5 ± 1.0 µM (n = 3); (ii) with 1000 nM L still present, mean [M] was 8.2 µM at 5 min, 3.0 µM at 10 min and 0.8 µM at 30 min.

Figure 1. Experimental set-up.
Figure 2. biosensor images (brightness scaled to mean [M]).

subs.html: (a) Construct a graph of mean [M] ± SD against [L], using equal spacing for each tenfold dose (plot 0 nM at the origin end of the axis).

key.rationale: axes labelled with variables and units, even spacing per decade (1); means plotted correctly (0.2, 0.9, 3.1, 7.8, 8.2) and connected, not extrapolated (1); error bars = SD (0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.7) (1).

subs.html: (b) Calculate the fold increase in mean [M] at 100 nM relative to 0 nM.
(c) A student claims, “The plateau shows that all receptors are occupied.” Evaluate this claim using observation (i).

key.rationale: claim not supported (1); [M] rises further (14.5) when the downstream enzyme is activated, so the plateau reflects a downstream limit rather than full receptor occupancy (1).

subs.html: (d) Propose one explanation for the fall in [M] in observation (ii) and describe an experiment to test it.

key.rationale: one explanation plus test, e.g. negative feedback or breakdown of M (phosphodiesterase) or receptor desensitization; add an inhibitor of M breakdown and see whether [M] stays high with L present.

subs.html: (e) Predict the effect of a competitive antagonist of L on [M] at 100 nM and 1000 nM, and justify.

key.rationale: a larger reduction at 100 nM than at 1000 nM because high L outcompetes a competitive antagonist.Common errors: using SD as “error” without computing it; concluding saturation means all receptors occupied.

cards.title: FRQ 3 (short)
cards.stim:
Compound Z was proposed to block signaling by receptor tyrosine kinase R. In a preliminary experiment, cells were treated with growth factor (GF), with or without Z (10 µM), and ERK-P, total ERK and viability were measured.

Figure 1. Candidate sites of action for Z.

subs.html: (a) Identify one reason the preliminary data do not yet show that Z inhibits R.

key.rationale: viability fell to 40% and total ERK fell (10 to 6), so lower ERK-P could reflect cell death or less ERK, not receptor inhibition.

subs.html: (b) Describe one change to the experiment that addresses your reason in (a).

key.rationale: normalize ERK-P to total ERK, and use a lower Z dose or shorter exposure that keeps viability near control, with a vehicle control.

subs.html: (c) Describe an experiment that would distinguish inhibition of R from inhibition of a downstream kinase.

key.rationale: e.g. measure receptor autophosphorylation, or treat cells expressing a constitutively active downstream kinase with Z and measure ERK-P.

subs.html: (d) Predict the result of your experiment in (c) if Z acts directly on R, and justify.

key.rationale: receptor autophosphorylation falls with Z, while ERK-P in cells with the active downstream kinase is unaffected, because Z acts upstream of the bypass.Common errors: proposing only a larger n; ignoring the viability data.

cards.title: FRQ 4 (short)
cards.stim:
A freshwater protist has a contractile vacuole. The cell interior is about 150 mOsm. A student concludes that the vacuole “actively pumps water out.”

Figure 1. One vacuole cycle.
Figure 2. Contraction rate (left) and cell volume after cyanide at 0 mOsm (right).

subs.html: (a) Explain why contraction rate falls as external solute concentration rises.

key.rationale: a smaller water-potential difference means less net water enters, so less must be expelled.

subs.html: (b) Explain the effect of cyanide on cell volume in terms of both water entry and ATP.

key.rationale: water keeps entering by osmosis while ATP-dependent expulsion stops, so volume rises.

subs.html: (c) Evaluate the student’s conclusion that water is actively pumped.

key.rationale: not supported: water moves by osmosis; the vacuole actively transports solutes (ions) into itself, and water follows.

subs.html: (d) A marine relative has no contractile vacuole. Justify why it does not need one.

key.rationale: seawater is isotonic or hypertonic to the cell, so little or no net water enters.Common errors: saying the cell “pumps water” without a solute gradient.

subs.html: (e) Sketch [1 pt]. Sketch the contraction rate you expect for a mutant with half as many functional vacuole pumps (WT values are in Figure 2). Label your curve “mutant”.

key.rationale: 1 pt: a decreasing curve that starts clearly below the WT value of 10 (about 5, reflecting reduced pumping capacity) and reaches 0 by about 150 mOsm.

cards.title: FRQ 5 (short)
cards.stim: In the model, receptor binding activates a G protein (GDP→GTP), which activates adenylyl cyclase to make cAMP; cAMP activates PKA, which phosphorylates CREB. Mutant A cannot hydrolyze GTP on the G protein. Mutant B has a receptor that cannot contact the G protein. At 1 nM ligand, 5% of WT receptors are occupied and cAMP is 60% of its maximum.

subs.html: (a) Explain, using the model, why Mutant A has high cAMP without ligand.

key.rationale: the G protein stays in the GTP-bound active state, so adenylyl cyclase keeps making cAMP without ligand.

subs.html: (b) Explain why ligand does not raise cAMP in Mutant B.

key.rationale: ligand can bind, but the receptor cannot activate the G protein, so the cascade is not started.

subs.html: (c) Justify that the pathway amplifies the signal, using the occupancy information.

key.rationale: 5% occupancy gives 60% of maximal cAMP, so each occupied receptor leads to many cAMP molecules.

subs.html: (d) A student claims, “Mutant A proves cAMP alone is sufficient to activate CREB targets.” Evaluate this claim and describe a test.

key.rationale: not shown: an active G protein has other effects; test by giving a cell-permeable cAMP analog to Mutant B (or a PKA inhibitor to Mutant A) and measuring CREB targets.Common errors: naming the receptor as the second messenger.

subs.html: (e) Draw [1 pt]. Draw the pathway for Mutant B after ligand is added: draw an arrow for each step that still occurs and an X at the first step that fails.

key.rationale: 1 pt: ligand binding to the receptor is shown as occurring, the X is placed between the receptor and the G protein, and the downstream steps (adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, PKA, CREB) are shown as not activated.LigandReceptorG proteinAdenylyl cyclasecAMPPKAX

cards.title: FRQ 6 (short)
cards.stim: Two tubes each began with 25 µmol substrate. Tube 1 had 0.5 µg enzyme, and 25 µmol more substrate was added at 5 min. Tube 2 had 1.0 µg enzyme and no addition.

subs.html: (a) Calculate the initial rate for Tube 1 in µmol/min.
(b) Explain the plateau in Tube 1 using the response to added substrate, and state what the response rules out.

key.rationale: the plateau reflects substrate depletion; the rate resumes after substrate is added, so enzyme inactivation is ruled out.

subs.html: (c) Describe how the data from Tube 2 relate to the amount of enzyme and to the total product formed.

key.rationale: initial rate is about double (16 vs 8 µmol/min), but total product is about the same (about 25 µmol) because substrate is limiting.

subs.html: (d) Describe an experiment to test whether product inhibition contributes to the slowing, and state the expected result if it does.

key.rationale: start reactions with added product and compare initial rates with a no-product control; lower initial rate with product indicates inhibition.Common errors: attributing the plateau to denaturation; taking the slope over the whole 5 min.

subs.html: (e) Sketch [1 pt]. Sketch the product curve expected for Tube 1 if its enzyme had been irreversibly inactivated at 5 min (before the second substrate addition). Start from the data (product 24 µmol at 5 min).

key.rationale: 1 pt: the curve follows the original rise to about 24 µmol at 5 min, then stays flat (no resumption) after substrate is added.

cards.title: Olympiad FRQ (14 pts: 12 + 2 for the graph construction)
cards.stim:
Cells have a hypothetical kinase K that, when active, blocks the G1/S transition. Three models for what activates K: M1 low absolute ATP; M2 low mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨ); M3 a high AMP:ATP ratio. Adenylate kinase interconverts 2 ADP ⇌ ATP + AMP. Cells (with glucose) were treated for 1 h; K activity was measured with a reporter that leaves the nucleus when K is active. Mean, n = 4 cultures.

Figure 1. Where each treatment acts, and the candidate cues for K.
ConditionATP (% control)ΔΨ (% control)AMP:ATPK activity (a.u.)
Control1001000.051.0
Oligomycin851300.081.3
FCCP80300.305.5
2-deoxyglucose601050.284.8
Figure 2. K-reporter images (green leaves the nucleus when K is active).
Figure 3. DNA content 24 h later (population flow cytometry; CA-K = constitutively active K; K-null = K deleted; KI = K inhibitor).

subs.html: (a) Identify which measured variable best tracks K activity across all four conditions and justify by comparing oligomycin with FCCP.

key.rationale: AMP:ATP (1); oligomycin and FCCP have similar ATP (85 vs 80) and ranking by ΔΨ is opposite, yet K differs 4-fold, matching the AMP:ATP change (0.08 vs 0.30) (1).
key.unit: Olympiad FRQ (14 pts: 12 + 2 for the graph construction)

subs.html: (b) Evaluate M1 and M2: cite one result inconsistent with each.

key.rationale: M1: FCCP (ATP 80) gives much higher K than oligomycin (ATP 85), and 2-DG (ATP 60) has lower K than FCCP (1). M2: 2-DG has near-normal ΔΨ (105%) but K is 4.8, and oligomycin raises ΔΨ without raising K (1).
key.unit: Olympiad FRQ (14 pts: 12 + 2 for the graph construction)

subs.html: (c) Calculate the fold change in K activity and the percent change in ΔΨ for FCCP relative to control.

key.unit: Olympiad FRQ (14 pts: 12 + 2 for the graph construction)

subs.html: (d) Explain why AMP:ATP can rise sharply when ATP falls only modestly.

key.rationale: ATP is a large pool; adenylate kinase converts a small ATP fall into a proportionally much larger AMP rise, so the ratio changes a lot.
key.unit: Olympiad FRQ (14 pts: 12 + 2 for the graph construction)

subs.html: (e) Evaluate the claim that K is necessary and sufficient for the G1 arrest, citing Figure 3.

key.rationale: necessary: K-null or KI cells treated with FCCP do not arrest (53–55% G1) (1); sufficient: CA-K arrests without stress (82% G1), though population data cannot show single-cell sufficiency (1).
key.unit: Olympiad FRQ (14 pts: 12 + 2 for the graph construction)

subs.html: (f) Propose an experiment that would separate M3 from M2 independently of the 2-DG result, and state the outcome that supports M3.

key.rationale: hold ΔΨ low while keeping AMP:ATP normal (or raise AMP:ATP without changing ΔΨ), e.g. FCCP with excess glycolytic ATP supply (1); M3 supported if K stays low when AMP:ATP is normal despite low ΔΨ (1).
key.unit: Olympiad FRQ (14 pts: 12 + 2 for the graph construction)

subs.html: (g) Predict K activity and G1 fraction under FCCP in cells whose K cannot bind AMP, and justify.

key.rationale: K stays low and G1 near control, since the cue cannot be read.
key.unit: Olympiad FRQ (14 pts: 12 + 2 for the graph construction)

subs.html: (h) Identify one limitation of the flow-cytometry data and a way to address it.

key.rationale: population average hides single-cell responses; time-lapse imaging of reporter and DNA content in single cells.Common errors: treating correlation of K with AMP:ATP as proof of direct binding; reading overlapping ATP values as identical.
key.unit: Olympiad FRQ (14 pts: 12 + 2 for the graph construction)

subs.html: (i) Construct [2 pts]. Construct a scatter plot of K activity (y) against AMP:ATP (x) for the four conditions in the table, and draw a best-fit line.

key.rationale: 1 pt: axes labelled with variables, even scales, and all four points plotted accurately (0.05, 1.0), (0.08, 1.3), (0.28, 4.8), (0.30, 5.5); 1 pt: an increasing best-fit line through the trend, not joining the dots point to point.
key.unit: Olympiad FRQ (14 pts: 12 + 2 for the graph construction)
